title: What is an anonymous class, when do you use it, what are its restrictions (no constructor, no static members, single base type), and how does it compare to lambdas?
shortTitle: Anonymous classes: what they are, when to use them, their restrictions, and how they compare to lambdas
keyPoints: An anonymous class is a nameless, one-shot class declared and instantiated inline with `new Type() { body }`.
It can extend exactly one class or implement exactly one interface, never both at the same time.
It cannot declare an explicit constructor because it has no name to attach one to.
It cannot declare static members other than compile-time constant `static final` fields.
Captured local variables must be effectively final because the anonymous instance holds a copy.
A lambda targets a single-abstract-method functional interface; an anonymous class handles multi-method interfaces or class extension.
Inside an anonymous class `this` refers to the anonymous object; inside a lambda `this` refers to the enclosing instance.

s1_definition.oneliner: An anonymous class is a nameless, one-shot subclass or interface implementation written inline where it is used, with no constructor and no instance static members.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Anonymous class** – a local class with no name, declared and instantiated in a single `new Type() { ... }` expression.
- **Single base type** – it extends exactly one class or implements exactly one interface, never both, and never more than one interface.
- **No explicit constructor** – because the class has no name, you cannot write a constructor; use an instance initializer `{{ }}` block instead.
- **No static members** – only compile-time constant `static final` fields are allowed; static methods and mutable static fields are forbidden.
- **Effectively-final capture** – local variables referenced from the anonymous body must be `final` or effectively final, because they are copied into the instance.
- **Compiled class file** – the compiler generates a numbered class file such as `Outer$1.class` for each anonymous class.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India and needs a one-time signatory for a single cheque. Instead of hiring a permanent, named employee for that one task, the branch manager grabs any available person, hands them a form with the exact instructions written on it, and that person signs just this once and is never seen again. There is no need to give that temporary helper a name, a job title, or a desk. That throwaway, nameless, one-task helper is an anonymous class.

sections.s6_takeaway:
An anonymous class is a local class without a name that you declare and instantiate in one expression. It extends exactly one class or implements exactly one interface, with the implementation written inline at the point of use. Its defining restrictions are that it cannot declare an explicit constructor because it has no name, it cannot declare static members other than compile-time constants, and it may capture only effectively-final local variables from the enclosing method.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, anonymous classes appear wherever Rajesh needs a one-off listener or callback with more than one method. A transfer listener with onStart and onComplete cannot be a lambda because it has two abstract methods, so an anonymous class supplies both methods inline. For single-method callbacks like a result handler, a lambda is shorter and clearer.

The comparison with lambdas is the part interviewers focus on. A lambda can only target a functional interface, meaning one abstract method, whereas an anonymous class can implement a multi-method interface or extend a concrete class. Inside an anonymous class `this` refers to the anonymous object, but inside a lambda `this` refers to the enclosing instance, which matters when you need the implementation object's own identity. Lambdas are also lighter at runtime because the compiler uses `invokedynamic` rather than always generating a separate class file.

The practical rule is straightforward. If the target is a functional interface and you just need a small piece of behaviour, write a lambda. If the interface has multiple methods, if you must extend a class, or if you need the implementation object's own `this`, write an anonymous class. This keeps the code concise where it can be and correct where it must be.

Remember one sentence: an anonymous class is a nameless, one-shot subclass or interface implementation declared inline, restricted to a single base type with no constructor and no static members, and you prefer a lambda whenever the target is a functional interface.
